Gastroenterology · published research

Dysphagia

Summary of the Evidence

Six publications are relevant: two randomized trials in cancer supportive care, two case reports, one three-case series, and one position paper. Dysphagia or swallowing was a secondary outcome in both trials. The reports address different causes and protocols, and the position paper synthesizes evidence rather than adding an independent patient cohort (Gautam et al. 2012; Legouté et al. 2019; Robijns et al. 2022).

Human and clinical evidence

A triple-blind randomized trial in 221 people receiving chemoradiotherapy for head-and-neck cancer reported lower dysphagia scores with prophylactic 633-nm laser alongside less severe oral mucositis, pain, and opioid use. Because the intervention and primary focus concerned mucositis, the result applies to dysphagia in that treatment context rather than swallowing disorders generally (Gautam et al. 2012).

A later multicentre randomized trial assigned 97 people with grade 2 or 3 oral mucositis during radiotherapy to 658-nm PBM or sham. Eighty-three were assessable, and the swallowing quality-of-life dimension did not differ between groups. The trial treated established mucositis and therefore tested a different setting from prophylaxis (Legouté et al. 2019).

One case report described improved swallowing after five daily 980-nm PBM sessions in a patient with chronic dysphagia following breast-cancer hormonal therapy. A separate three-case cancer-complication series included one dysphagia case treated with 635-nm PBM. These uncontrolled observations cannot separate treatment effects from recovery or co-interventions (El Mobadder et al. 2019a; El Mobadder et al. 2019b).

Another exact-category case used water-filtered infrared-A on the neck and chest together with acetylcysteine. Oral intake improved over time, but the intervention was heat-producing infrared and the co-treatment prevents attribution to light alone (Hoffmann et al. 2017).

Animal evidence

No animal study directly examining PBM for dysphagia was identified in these records.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The prophylaxis trial used 632.8-nm red helium-neon laser, 3 J per point and 36–40 J per session, five days per week during chemoradiotherapy. The multicentre treatment trial used 658 nm, 100 mW, and 4 J/cm². The single PBM case used 980 nm at 3 J per point over five days, while the case series used 635 nm. The wIRA case was a distinct thermal modality. These protocols target different causes and tissues and have not been compared directly.

Interpretation

The randomized findings are mixed: one prophylaxis trial reported less dysphagia, while a later trial treating established mucositis found no benefit in its swallowing quality-of-life dimension. The 2022 WALT position paper places dysphagia within cancer-supportive-care guidance but does not remove uncertainty from the mixed secondary outcomes (Robijns et al. 2022). Evidence remains low for chemoradiotherapy-associated mucositis and very low for other causes, with no basis for generalizing to neurologic or structural dysphagia.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

One 221-person triple-blind trial reported less dysphagia with prophylactic 633-nm laser during chemoradiotherapy, but a later multicentre trial found no benefit in the swallowing quality-of-life dimension when 658-nm PBM treated established mucositis. Case reports and a small series are uncontrolled, and one exact-category case used thermal wIRA with acetylcysteine. These limitations support low certainty in the mucositis context and very low certainty elsewhere.
